## {#today .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.todaymeta}
Three days · four sessions of ninety minutes a day
:::

:::: {.todaybox}
::: {.nonincremental}
1. Day 1 – The tools: credibility as a software problem, the toolchain walked slowly, and a first session in R
2. Day 2 – The workshop: the claim, its estimand and its graph; the reproduction; the menu; the multiverse and the declaration
3. Day 3 – The methods in depth: every axis of the menu, the multiverse and its critics, reading a curve, and where the work is archived
:::
::::

::: {.todaytake}
You leave with: a reproducible workspace you can drive · a reproduced result · an estimand and a DAG of your own · a preregistered analysis on the class curve · the methods behind every choice you made
:::

::: {.todaymeta}
Work along in your IDE, or on the browser lab page – solo or in pairs
:::

::: notes
Three days, and the deck follows them in order. Day one is the tools, taken slowly, and ends with everyone running. Day two is the workshop day as it runs on its own, in four parts. Day three goes back through the methods that day two had to take at speed, in the order they were needed, and ends on where a finished piece of work goes to live.
:::

::: {.partlabel}
Day 1 · four sessions

::: notes
Day one. What science is for and why anyone thinks it is in trouble, the evidence, and five analysts of one claim who all shipped runnable code. Then the toolchain, walked slowly – languages, editors, plain text, rendering, packages, version control, archives, licences – and a first session in R in the workspace, so that tomorrow opens on the paper with the installation behind us.
:::

# DAY 3 – The methods in depth {.darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Day 3 · four sessions
:::

::: notes
Day three slows down everything that yesterday took at speed. Every axis of the menu, shown doing something to an estimate; where the multiverse idea came from and what it is for; why hundreds of estimates are not hundreds of tests and what a curve-level test would have to do; and then where a finished reanalysis is archived and registered. The companion modules carry the rest of the day – the graphs, the estimators output by output, weights, missing answers, simulation and version control.
:::
